domain_label: Scheduling & Spaced Repetition — Timeline Planning Back From an Exam Date (Anki/SM-2/FSRS)
purpose: A method for planning a spaced-repetition study timeline backwards from a fixed exam date: sizing the card deck against the days available, shaping a sustainable daily review load, choosing a deadline-constrained retention target, pacing new-card introduction against the review debt each new card creates, setting a last-day-to-learn cutoff, absorbing backlog/overdue spikes and lapse/relearning load, interleaving two exams in parallel (a dental board plus TOEFL) inside one daily time budget, and closing with a feasibility go/no-go — grounding every scheduler-mechanics claim in Anki/SM-2/FSRS source-of-record facts and tagging every back-planning heuristic as an estimate rather than a fabricated formula.
assumptions: no live per-user revlog or fitted FSRS parameter vector is supplied; every workload projection is a labeled estimate built on the published FSRS default parameters and the documented desired-retention/interval identity, never a promise of a specific pass date

the two concrete deadlines are a dental board exam and a TOEFL sitting studied in parallel; their absolute card counts, the learner's true daily minutes and the learner's fitted memory parameters are all treated as inputs to be measured, not invented

scheduler mechanics (SM-2 constants, classic-Anki deltas, FSRS DSR formulas, fuzz, revlog shape) are FACTs sourced from Anki's own FAQ/manual/source repos and the official FSRS algorithm wiki; back-timeline shaping (retention ramps, cutoff offsets, new-card tapers, time-split ratios) is design synthesis tagged ESTIMATE

there is no verified closed-form 'days-to-mastery' equation in the sources; reaching a target retention across a whole deck by a date is obtained by simulation (FSRS simulator / Compute-Minimum-Recommended-Retention) or by conservative estimate, not by a single algebraic formula

absolute forgetting-curve magnitudes from primary literature (Ebbinghaus figures, Cepeda optimal-gap numbers) were unreachable this session and are held UNKNOWN; only the qualitative spacing/testing effects and the fetched Rea&Modigliani / Donovan&Radosevich numbers are used
exclusions: the internal derivation and per-grade arithmetic of the memory algorithms beyond what timeline planning consumes (the full SM-2 vs classic-Anki vs FSRS mechanics belong to the algorithms KB); this KB uses their scheduling behaviour, not their proofs
card authoring, note-type/template design, media handling and content quality (a separate content KB); this KB schedules whatever cards exist, it does not write them
the pedagogy of what to study or item atomicity beyond the fact that each card is both a test and a spaced exposure

app-specific UI walkthroughs and add-on installation steps beyond naming the deck-option knobs (desired retention, new/review limits, learning steps, New Interval, maximum interval) and the interop actions the plan relies on
fabricating a pass probability, an exam pass rate, a specific optimal desired-retention number for a named exam, or a days-to-mastery formula the sources do not verify

competency_questions.question: What state and inputs does any scheduler need, and why must a timeline plan treat scheduling as a (grade, elapsed-time) -> next-interval function rather than a fixed calendar?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SCHEDULER_STATE_MODEL states SM-2 state (EF,n,last-interval) vs FSRS memory state (D,S), that both consume a grade and elapsed time, that SM-2 ignores actual elapsed time while FSRS takes it natively, and FORGETTING_CURVE_BACKBONE states S = the interval at which recall probability R = 90% and that R decays with time between reviews

competency_questions.question: Why is desired retention the single workload knob, and how does raising it toward a deadline trade study time for recall?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: RETENTION_WORKLOAD_KNOB gives the interval = inverse-forgetting-curve identity (I(0.9,S)=S; default 0.90; workload rises fast above 90% and can be overwhelming above 97%) and DEADLINE_RETENTION_TARGET frames raising retention near the exam as a deliberate, time-costly choice bounded by the workload-minimizing retention (CMRR), tagging the ramp shape estimate

competency_questions.question: How is the plan anchored to the exam date, and what does counting cards against days-available tell you before any daily numbers?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: EXAM_DATE_ANCHOR fixes the exam date and days-available as the back-planning origin and states there is no verified days-to-mastery formula, while DECK_SIZING_INVENTORY counts total/new/known cards so the deck-vs-days ratio surfaces feasibility, both flagging the counts as measured inputs

competency_questions.question: What is the steady-state daily review load a deck settles into, and how is the daily load shaped so it does not spike?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: STEADY_STATE_LOAD_MATH explains that at desired retention r each mature card recurs on the order of its interval so daily reviews scale with deck size / average interval and new cards each add a recurring review stream, and DAILY_REVIEW_LOAD_SHAPING sets new/review daily caps to keep the load bounded, both tagged estimate on the projection

competency_questions.question: How fast should new cards be introduced given that each new card creates a lasting review debt, and what caps the rate?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NEW_CARD_INTRODUCTION_RATE states each new card graduates into a recurring review stream so the sustainable new-card/day is bounded by the review load and time budget it will generate weeks later, not by the day it is introduced

competency_questions.question: When must new-card introduction stop before the exam so every card gets enough exposure, and how is that cutoff derived?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: NEW_CARD_CUTOFF_DATE sets a last-day-to-learn offset before the exam so no card is seen only once, derives it from the learning steps and first review intervals, and tags the specific offset an estimate to confirm against the deck's actual short intervals

competency_questions.question: How is a backlog of overdue reviews absorbed without a load spike, and why does late-answer credit and fuzz matter to the plan?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: BACKLOG_OVERDUE_HANDLING describes capping daily reviews and draining overdue over several days (Anki credits days-late into the next interval so overdue-but-recalled cards are not wasted) and LOAD_SMOOTHING_FUZZ explains the built-in, non-disable-able fuzz that spreads same-day cohorts to prevent recurring clumps

competency_questions.question: How much daily capacity must be reserved for lapses and relearning, and how are leeches handled?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: LAPSE_RELEARN_BUDGET states that a lapse sends a card to relearning (classic Anki multiplies the interval by New Interval, default full reset) adding near-term reviews, that repeated lapses flag a leech to suspend/tag, and that the plan reserves headroom for this churn rather than budgeting only first-pass reviews

competency_questions.question: How are two exams (dental board + TOEFL) interleaved inside one daily time budget, and what governs the split?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MULTI_EXAM_INTERLEAVING keeps the two decks as separate presets with their own retention/limits, splits the shared daily minutes by each exam's deck-size, days-remaining and per-card time, and TIME_BUDGET_CONSTRAINT states the minutes/day capacity that caps their combined new+review+relearn load

competency_questions.question: What is the role and the risk of final-week cramming / filtered decks and of reviewing ahead of schedule?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CRAM_FILTERED_DECK frames a filtered/cram deck as a bounded final-week exposure that boosts short-term recall but not durable stability (massed practice underperforms spaced), and AHEAD_OF_SCHEDULE_REVIEW explains that answering early shortens the effective interval and wastes workload for little stability gain, so both are used sparingly

competency_questions.question: What must be logged from day one, and how are per-user scheduler parameters obtained rather than assumed?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: REVLOG_TELEMETRY specifies logging every review in revlog shape (timestamp_ms, item_id, grade 1-4, interval, last_interval, duration_ms, type) and PARAMETER_OPTIMIZATION states the FSRS w-vector is fitted per user from that revlog by maximum-likelihood (about monthly, not hand-edited) and is UNKNOWN until enough history exists, so early projections use published defaults

competency_questions.question: How is progress tracked against the timeline, when is the plan replanned, and what makes the whole timeline a go or a no-go?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: PROGRESS_BURNDOWN tracks remaining new cards and knowledge (~ sum of per-card R) against the days left, CONTINGENCY_REPLAN names the triggers (falling behind, load spikes, lapse churn) and the levers to pull, and PLAN_GO_NOGO composes deck-vs-days, time budget, cutoff feasibility, the multi-exam split and cram posture into a feasible/infeasible verdict

glossary.definition: The target probability of recalling a card at review time; the single knob that sets workload. Interval is the inverse forgetting curve at this value, so I(0.9,S)=S by construction. Anki default is 0.90; the manual warns workload rises quickly above 90% and can be overwhelming above 97% [FACT — Anki deck-options manual].

In the FSRS DSR model, the number of days for recall probability R to fall from 100% to 90%; i.e. S is the interval at which R=90%. It grows after each successful review (the spacing effect) with a bounded, not linear, gain for overdue-but-recalled cards [FACT — official FSRS algorithm wiki].

The probability of recalling a card right now; it decays with elapsed time since the last review along the power forgetting curve R(t,S)=(1+factor*t/S)^(-w20). It is the only DSR component that changes without a review; whole-deck 'knowledge' is approximated by the sum of R across cards [FACT — FSRS wiki + fsrs4anki optimal-retention wiki].

The original SuperMemo-2 schedule Anki descends from: E-Factor starts at 2.5, I(1)=1 day, I(2)=6 days, I(n)=I(n-1)*EF for n>2, EF floored at 1.3, and a failure (grade q<3) restarts the interval ladder. SM-2 ignores how late a review actually was [FACT — Anki FAQ + SM-2 mirror].

Classic Anki's patch for SM-2's blind spot: answering later than scheduled is factored into the next interval (Good uses (current_interval + days_late/2)*ease; Easy uses (current_interval + days_late)*ease*bonus), so draining an overdue backlog of still-recalled cards is not wasted effort [FACT — Anki scheduler source review.rs].

The design fact that introducing one new card is not a one-day cost: after it graduates it recurs indefinitely at its growing interval, so N new cards/day compounds into a rising review stream weeks later. The sustainable new-card rate is therefore bounded by the future review+time load it creates, not by today's capacity [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the interval mechanics].

The date before the exam after which no new cards are introduced, so every card gets at least its learning steps plus one or two spaced reviews rather than being seen once. Derived from the deck's learning steps and first review intervals; the exact offset is an estimate to confirm against the actual short intervals [ESTIMATE — design synthesis].

A card that lapses repeatedly (Anki's default threshold flags it) and is auto-suspended or tagged; in timeline terms a small set of leeches consumes disproportionate relearning capacity and should be reformulated or set aside rather than allowed to inflate daily load [FACT — Anki deck-options manual, Leeches].

The random jitter Anki adds to every interval (roughly +/-(1 day + 15% of days in 2.5-7, 10% in 7-20, 5% beyond); short intervals not fuzzed; cannot be disabled) so that cards introduced together and graded alike do not resurface as a recurring same-day clump [FACT — Anki studying manual + fuzz.rs source].

The one-row-per-review log (timestamp_ms, card/item id, grade 1-4, new interval, previous interval, duration_ms capped at 60s, type learn/review/relearn/cram) that both the FSRS optimizer consumes to fit per-user parameters and Anki accepts via insertReviews; logging in this shape from day one keeps the plan optimizable and portable [FACT — AnkiDroid DB schema + AnkiConnect + FSRS optimization wiki].

Anki's search for the workload-minimizing desired retention, reflecting that workload vs retention is U-shaped (too-high retention means too many reviews; too-low means too much relearning). Setting retention below the CMRR is dominated — more time and less knowledge — so it is the floor a deadline plan reasons around [FACT — fsrs4anki optimal-retention wiki + deck-options manual].

nodes.definition: Establish the object every timeline plan schedules against: a scheduler is a pure function (grade, elapsed-time) -> (next memory state, next interval). SM-2's state is (E-Factor, repetition count n, last interval) with EF starting 2.5 and a q<3 failure restarting the ladder; classic Anki keeps an SM-2-style ease (initial 2.5, floor 1.3, deltas Again -0.20 / Hard -0.15 / Good 0 / Easy +0.15) [FACT — Anki FAQ + review.rs]. FSRS's state is a two-number memory state (Difficulty D in [1,10], Stability S) with grades 1=again..4=easy and next_states(prev_state, desired_retention, elapsed_days) returning one candidate per button [FACT — fsrs-rs README]. The load-bearing point for planning: both response (grade) and time (elapsed) are mandatory inputs; SM-2 ignores actual elapsed time, classic Anki patched that with days-late credit, and FSRS handles it natively with a bounded stability gain. A calendar that assumes fixed dates is therefore wrong — due dates move with grades.

included: the (grade, elapsed) -> next-state/interval abstraction
SM-2 vs classic-Anki vs FSRS state contents
the mandatory grade-and-time inputs and SM-2's elapsed-time blind spot
excluded: the full per-grade arithmetic of each algorithm
card content and note-type design

pros.claim: Modeling scheduling as a grade-and-time function stops the plan being built as a fixed wall-calendar that the first wrong answer invalidates
pros.example: treating a card's next due date as recomputed from its grade and lateness rather than pinned to a spreadsheet cell

cons.claim: The abstraction hides algorithm-specific behaviour that changes projected load (SM-2 geometric growth vs FSRS bounded stability gain)
cons.example: assuming SM-2-style unbounded interval growth when the deck runs FSRS and intervals plateau differently

failure_modes: planning against fixed calendar dates that ignore that grades move due dates
assuming one algorithm's growth behaviour while the deck runs another
acceptance_tests: the analysis states the (grade, elapsed) -> next-state/interval function, contrasts SM-2 (EF,n,interval) with FSRS (D,S), and names elapsed time as a mandatory input SM-2 ignores
revisit_triggers: the deck switches scheduler (classic Anki <-> FSRS)
a new scheduler version changes the state variables

nodes.definition: Fix the memory backbone the whole timeline math rests on. Retrievability R is the probability of recall now and decays with elapsed time; Stability S is the interval at which R falls to 90% (S = interval where R=0.9). FSRS-6 uses a trainable power forgetting curve R(t,S)=(1+factor*t/S)^(-w20) with factor=0.9^(-1/w20)-1 so that R(S,S)=0.9 [FACT — official FSRS algorithm wiki]. Each successful review raises S (the spacing effect: the stability gain is larger when R has dropped lower), and for overdue-but-recalled cards the gain converges to a bound rather than growing linearly as SM-2/classic-Anki would [FACT — FSRS wiki]. Whole-deck knowledge is approximated as the sum of R across cards [FACT — fsrs4anki optimal-retention wiki]. The qualitative spacing and testing effects are well established (Rea & Modigliani 1985: 70% vs 53% recall distributed vs massed; Donovan & Radosevich 1999 meta-analytic effect size 0.46 favouring spaced) [FACT — fetched], but the absolute primary-source magnitudes (Ebbinghaus's exact figures, Cepeda's optimal-gap numbers) are [UNKNOWN — primary texts unreachable this session], so the curve is used for shape, not for a promised recall percentage on a given day.

the power forgetting curve and the bounded stability gain

excluded: the full per-grade stability-update formulas

pros.claim: Defining S as the interval where R=90% makes desired retention and interval two views of one quantity, which is what makes a timeline computable
pros.example: reading a card's stability directly as 'days until it decays to 90% recall' when spacing the next review

cons.claim: Using default-parameter curves for an individual over-promises precision the primary literature does not verify and the user's own parameters are not yet fitted
cons.example: quoting a specific recall % for a card on exam day from default parameters before any personal revlog exists

failure_modes: treating a default-parameter curve as a personal guarantee of recall on a date
citing unverified absolute forgetting figures as if fetched
acceptance_tests: the analysis states R decays with time, S = the interval at which R=90%, that stability gain is bounded for overdue cards, and that absolute primary-source magnitudes are UNKNOWN while the spacing/testing effect direction is FACT

base.update_signal: an FSRS curve/parameter change or a reachable primary source updates the backbone

nodes.definition: Establish desired retention as the one dial that trades study time for recall, because interval is the inverse forgetting curve at the chosen retention r: I(r,S)=(S/factor)*(r^(-1/w20)-1), with I(0.9,S)=S by construction [FACT — FSRS wiki]. Higher r shortens every interval and multiplies reviews/day; lower r lengthens intervals but causes more forgetting and relearning, so the relationship is U-shaped, not monotone, and Anki's Compute-Minimum-Recommended-Retention searches for the workload-minimizing point [FACT — deck-options + optimal-retention wiki]. Anki defaults to 0.90 and warns workload rises very quickly above 90% and can be overwhelming above 97%. The classic-Anki equivalent is the interval modifier new_modifier = log(desired)/log(current); raising 85% to 90% gives ~0.65, i.e. about 35% more reviews for +5 points of retention — a concrete, non-linear price [FACT — deck-options manual]. This node makes retention the primary lever every downstream load number reads from.

included: the interval = inverse-curve-at-r identity and I(0.9,S)=S
the U-shaped workload-vs-retention curve and CMRR floor
the 0.90 default, the >97% warning, and the log-ratio interval-modifier equivalent
excluded: the deadline-driven decision of which retention to pick (its own node)
per-user parameter fitting

pros.claim: Naming retention as the single knob lets the plan turn 'study harder' into a quantified reviews-per-day change instead of a vibe
pros.example: showing that moving 85% to 90% is ~35% more reviews so a busy learner sees the real cost before choosing

cons.claim: Because workload is U-shaped, naive 'raise retention to be safe' pushes into the steep zone above 90% where a small gain costs a large load
cons.example: setting 97% retention for safety and generating an unsustainable daily review count

failure_modes: pushing retention above ~90% without accounting for the fast-rising workload
setting retention below the CMRR and getting more work for less knowledge
acceptance_tests: the analysis gives the interval = inverse-curve-at-r identity, the U-shaped workload relationship with the CMRR floor, the 0.90 default and >97% warning, and the log-ratio interval-modifier cost of +5 points
revisit_triggers: the deadline forces a retention change (handled downstream)
CMRR output shifts after re-optimization
the workload from a chosen retention proves unsustainable in practice

base.update_signal: a CMRR shift or an unsustainable observed workload changes the retention lever

nodes.definition: Anchor the entire plan to the fixed exam date and the days-available count, and back-plan from it. The exam date is the hard constraint every other quantity is measured against; days-available = calendar days minus expected off-days is the budget the deck must fit inside. The load-bearing honesty point: the sources give an exact retention<->interval identity but NO verified closed-form 'days to master N cards to retention r' equation, so the time to bring a whole deck to a target retention by a date is obtained by simulation (FSRS simulator / CMRR) or by conservative estimate, never by an invented formula [ESTIMATE — design synthesis; the absence of a closed form is grounded in the sources]. For the two concrete deadlines (a dental board exam and a TOEFL sitting), each gets its own anchor date and its own days-available, which the multi-exam split later reconciles. This node deliberately produces only the origin and the budget; it hands the card counting and daily numbers to downstream nodes.

included: the fixed exam date and days-available as the back-planning origin
the explicit absence of a verified days-to-mastery formula and the simulate-or-estimate rule
a separate anchor per exam (dental board, TOEFL)
excluded: the card inventory itself (its own node)
the daily review-load math

pros.claim: Fixing the date and days-available first prevents planning daily numbers that silently assume more calendar than exists
pros.example: discovering at the anchor step that only 60 study days remain before committing to a new-card rate

cons.claim: Days-available is itself an estimate of off-days that can be optimistic and shrink the real budget
cons.example: assuming zero sick or travel days and over-committing the schedule

failure_modes: planning from today forward until 'done' instead of back from the fixed date
quoting an invented days-to-mastery formula instead of simulating or estimating
acceptance_tests: the plan states the exam date and days-available as the origin, notes there is no verified days-to-mastery formula so time-to-target is simulated or estimated, and gives each exam its own anchor
revisit_triggers: the exam date moves or is confirmed

base.update_signal: an exam-date move or an off-day revision changes the anchor and budget

nodes.definition: Count the deck against the anchor: total cards, the new (never-studied) subset, the already-learning/review subset, and any expected additions, so the deck-vs-days ratio is explicit before any daily number is chosen. The new-card count divided by days-available (net of the last-day-to-learn cutoff) gives the minimum new-cards-per-day the timeline demands; the mature-card count drives the recurring review baseline. For the dental board a large fact deck and for TOEFL a smaller vocabulary/idiom deck are sized separately, because their counts, per-card difficulty and days-remaining differ. The counts are measured inputs, never guessed: an unknown deck size makes every downstream projection unfalsifiable, so this node insists on an actual card count (from the collection or the source material) and flags any estimated portion. It produces the inventory the load math and the new-card rate consume.

the new-cards-over-days minimum-rate ratio and the mature-card review baseline
a separate inventory per exam deck
excluded: the sustainable new-card rate decision (its own node)

nodes.definition: Establish the daily time budget as the hard capacity the whole plan must fit under: minutes-available/day times cards-per-minute throughput = the maximum new + review + relearn cards the learner can actually clear. Anki caps per-review duration at 60s in the revlog, but real throughput is measured, not assumed, and differs by deck (clinical reasoning cards are slower than vocab recognition). This budget is what turns retention and new-card choices from abstractions into a feasibility test: if the projected steady-state load exceeds the budget, either retention, new-card rate, or the deadline must give. For two exams in parallel it is a single shared budget both decks draw from, which the multi-exam split allocates. The time budget, not card count, is the usual true bottleneck, so it is surfaced early and revisited whenever the observed daily minutes drift from the assumption.

throughput as a measured, deck-specific quantity
one shared budget across parallel exams as the feasibility ceiling
excluded: the allocation of the budget between two exams (its own node)

nodes.definition: Project the recurring daily review load a deck settles into, so the plan is sized for the plateau, not the first week. At desired retention r a mature card recurs roughly every S-scaled interval, so daily mature reviews scale on the order of (number of mature cards) / (average interval in days): a large deck with short average intervals generates a heavy standing review stream even with zero new cards. Each new card graduated adds its own recurring stream, so steady-state reviews/day grow with cumulative cards introduced and shrink as intervals lengthen. This is the number that, compared against the time budget, decides feasibility. Because the true intervals depend on the user's fitted parameters (not yet known early on), the projection is an ESTIMATE using published FSRS defaults or an Anki simulation, explicitly labeled, and refined once revlog exists. It feeds the daily-load shaping and the new-card rate.

excluded: the setting of daily caps (its own node)

nodes.definition: Set the new-cards-per-day rate on the principle that a new card is a recurring liability, not a one-day cost: once it graduates it recurs indefinitely at its growing interval, so N new/day compounds into a rising review stream weeks later [ESTIMATE — design synthesis over the interval mechanics]. The sustainable rate is therefore bounded from above by the steady-state review load and time budget the card will generate, and from below by the deck-vs-days minimum from inventory. The plan reconciles the two: if the deadline's minimum new/day exceeds the sustainable rate, the timeline is infeasible as posed and something must give (more time/day, lower retention, fewer cards, later new content). A common shape is to front-load new cards early (so they mature before the exam) and taper them toward the cutoff, keeping the compounding review debt inside the budget. This rate is the master pacing lever the daily-load shaping and cutoff date build on.

nodes.definition: Turn the projected load into a shaped daily schedule by setting the deck-option caps (new-cards/day and maximum-reviews/day) and a target session length that keep each day inside the time budget while still draining the deck by the exam. The art is smoothing: a hard reviews/day cap protects against spike days but, if set below the true recurring demand, silently defers reviews into a growing overdue pile, so the cap must be at least the steady-state plateau plus lapse headroom. Shaping also means front-loading new cards and letting the review stream build early rather than stacking an unsurvivable crunch near the exam. This node produces the concrete daily targets (new N/day, reviews up to M/day, ~T minutes) that every execution node (backlog, lapses, fuzz, ahead-review, multi-exam) reads and adjusts. It is the operational center of the plan.

nodes.definition: Choose the desired retention for the deadline, deliberately rather than by default, given that retention is the workload knob and time is fixed. A defensible pattern is to hold a moderate retention (around the 0.90 default) through the bulk of the timeline for throughput, then, if capacity allows, nudge it up in the final stretch so cards are freshest at the exam — the ramp is an ESTIMATE (design synthesis), not a sourced schedule, and its size is bounded by the budget, never chosen 'to be safe'. nodes.definition: Set the last-day-to-learn cutoff: the date before the exam after which no new cards are introduced, so that every card gets at least its learning steps plus one or two spaced reviews instead of being seen once and forgotten. nodes.definition: Handle the overdue backlog that any missed day or over-tight review cap produces, without letting it spike or its cards go stale. The key mechanic is that Anki credits how late a review was into the next interval (Good uses (current_interval + days_late/2)*ease; Easy uses (current_interval + days_late)*ease*bonus), so an overdue-but-still-recalled card is not wasted effort and its next interval extends [FACT — review.rs]. nodes.definition: Reserve daily capacity for the relearning churn that lapses create, which first-pass planning ignores. When a review card is answered Again it enters relearning and its interval is multiplied by the New Interval setting (classic Anki default 0.00 = full reset, e.g. 0.20 keeps 20% of a 100-day interval), so a lapse adds near-term reviews on top of the standing load [FACT — deck-options manual]. Cards that lapse repeatedly are flagged as leeches (default threshold) and auto-suspended or tagged, and a handful of leeches can eat disproportionate capacity, so the plan reformulates or sets them aside rather than grinding them. nodes.definition: Use interval fuzz to keep the daily load smooth over the whole timeline instead of clumping. Anki applies random fuzz to every interval (roughly +/-(1 day + 15% of days in the 2.5-7 band, 10% in 7-20, 5% beyond); short intervals are not fuzzed) specifically so that cards introduced on the same day and graded the same do not resurface together as a recurring same-day spike; the fuzz cannot be disabled [FACT — studying manual + fuzz.rs]. For a deadline plan this matters twice: it naturally disperses a front-loaded new-card cohort so its reviews do not all land on one future day, and it means any homegrown or spreadsheet schedule must add similar jitter or it will manufacture avoidable load spikes. The planning takeaway is to trust the built-in fuzz, avoid deterministic same-day batching of large cohorts, and read residual clumping as a cohort-size problem rather than a scheduler fault. nodes.definition: Decide the policy on reviewing ahead of schedule, because it is a common instinct with a real cost. nodes.definition: Run two exams in parallel (a dental board exam and a TOEFL sitting) as separate decks with separate presets, and split the shared daily time budget between them. nodes.definition: Define the replanning move when the burndown shows the plan is off pace, so correction is a named procedure not a panic. Each lever has a modeled effect the burndown can re-project, and the choice is driven by which constraint is binding — time budget, deck size, or retention. edges.why_related: the (grade, elapsed) state model is what the retrievability/stability memory backbone instantiates
the forgetting curve and S = interval-at-R=90% are what make desired retention and interval two views of one quantity
the days-available budget is what the card inventory is counted against
the anchor's days frame the per-day minutes capacity the plan must fit under
the chosen retention sets the interval scale the steady-state review projection divides deck size by
the mature-card count is the numerator of the reviews-per-day projection
the new-cards-over-days ratio sets the lower bound on the new-card rate
the recurring load a graduated card adds is what upper-bounds the sustainable new-card rate
the projected plateau is the floor the daily review cap must sit at or above
the new-card rate is one of the two daily caps the schedule shapes
the retention<->workload identity is what the deadline-constrained target chooses a point on
the fixed date and budget are what make the retention choice a bounded deadline decision
the rate that fills the pre-cutoff window determines whether the deck can be introduced before the cutoff
the cutoff is an offset measured back from the fixed exam date
the review cap set by shaping is what determines whether and how a backlog forms and drains
the daily caps are what the lapse/relearning headroom is reserved on top of
the shaped daily targets are what fuzz keeps achievable by dispersing same-day cohorts
the spacing-effect stability behaviour is why early review (R still high) gives little gain
the daily capacity is what early review either protects (before an absence) or wastes
the single shared minutes budget is what the two-exam split allocates
each exam's shaped daily load is what the interleaving schedules against the other
cram is a post-cutoff, new-cards-stopped regime, so the cutoff precedes and bounds it
the final-stretch retention posture frames how much extra final-week exposure is warranted
the grade-and-interval state transitions are exactly what each revlog row records
the per-review log is the training data the FSRS optimizer fits the w-vector from
the DSR curve is the model whose 21 parameters the optimizer fits
the target retention is the knowledge line the sum-of-R burndown is measured against
the revlog is what lets the burndown use observed retention rather than assumed
the burndown divergence is the objective trigger the replan levers respond to
the available corrective levers are what turn a breached constraint into a conditional go
whether both exams fit the single budget is one of the constraints the verdict intersects
the bounded-cram posture is one of the do-not rules the verdict enforces
a faster new-card rate clears the deck sooner but inflates the future review load the daily shaping must bound
edges.resolution_rule: cap the new-card rate at the level whose matured review stream still fits the shaped daily budget; when they conflict the sustainable daily load wins over clearing the backlog faster

edges.why_related: a higher retention target shortens intervals and raises reviews/day, which can exceed the fixed daily time budget
edges.resolution_rule: keep retention between the CMRR floor and the point where projected load fits the budget; the time budget is the hard ceiling, so cap retention rather than overflow the minutes available

edges.why_related: final-week massed cramming pulls against the spacing effect that builds durable stability
edges.resolution_rule: use cram only as a bounded short-term-recall supplement for weak/high-yield cards and never as a substitute for the spaced review stream, because massed practice underperforms spaced immediately post-training and the durable-retention case rests on the spacing-effect direction plus the ESTIMATE-tagged testing effect

edges.why_related: two exams compete for the same new-card and time capacity, so each exam's desired new-card rate fights the other's
edges.resolution_rule: allocate new-card slots by each exam's deck-size and days-remaining under the shared budget; the nearer/larger exam gets priority until its deadline, then its capacity frees for the other

edges.why_related: reviewing early feels like extra safety but shortens effective intervals and wastes the workload the retention knob is meant to allocate efficiently
edges.resolution_rule: default to on-time review so capacity goes to cards near forgetting; permit early review only to cover a known absence or genuinely shaky cards, not as a routine safety habit

edges.why_related: the daily minutes ceiling caps how many new cards can be sustained once their reviews mature
a burst of lapses causally inflates the near-term review count that can tip a day into backlog
the observed burndown pace feeds back to raise or lower the new-card rate to stay on the fixed-date line

conflict_axes.name: coverage_speed_vs_sustainable_load
conflict_axes.description: Introducing new cards fast clears the deck sooner but compounds into a future review load that can exceed the daily budget.
poles: introduce new cards fast to finish the deck
cap new cards to a sustainable matured load
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: bound the new-card rate by the review+time load its matured cards will generate, front-load then taper, and let sustainable daily load win over fast backlog clearance

conflict_axes.name: retention_safety_vs_time_budget
conflict_axes.description: A higher retention target raises exam-day recall but shortens intervals and multiplies reviews/day beyond the fixed time budget, especially above 90%.
poles: hold retention to fit the budget
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep retention between the CMRR floor and the budget ceiling; never push above ~90% 'to be safe' when it overflows the minutes available

conflict_axes.name: cram_recall_vs_durable_stability
conflict_axes.description: Final-week massed cram lifts short-term recall for exam day but the spacing effect shows it builds little durable stability.
poles: cram the final week for the exam
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use bounded filtered-deck cram only for weak/high-yield cards on top of, never instead of, the spaced timeline

conflict_axes.name: two_exams_competing_for_one_budget
conflict_axes.description: A dental board and a TOEFL sitting draw on the same daily minutes, so each exam's ideal pace starves the other.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: split minutes by deck-size and days-remaining, give the nearer/larger exam priority until its deadline, then reallocate to the other while keeping both from going overdue

conflict_axes.name: cover_everything_vs_last_day_to_learn
conflict_axes.description: Introducing new cards up to the exam maximises coverage but leaves late cards seen only once; an early cutoff consolidates but drops scope.
poles: keep adding new cards to cover it all
stop new cards at a safe cutoff
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set the cutoff so every card gets at least one post-graduation review and cut low-yield scope rather than shipping cards seen only once

conflict_axes.name: on_time_review_vs_early_safety
conflict_axes.description: Reviewing early feels safer but wastes workload for little stability gain while R is still high.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: default to on-time so capacity targets cards near forgetting; reserve early review for a known absence or shaky cards

conflict_axes.name: hard_review_cap_vs_hidden_overdue_debt
conflict_axes.description: A low reviews/day cap protects a session but silently defers due cards into a growing overdue backlog.
poles: cap reviews low to protect the day
set the cap at the true recurring demand
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: set the review cap at least at the steady-state plateau plus lapse headroom, and drain any backlog deliberately rather than hiding it under a low cap

conflict_axes.name: default_parameters_vs_fitted_personal_model
conflict_axes.description: Early projections must use published FSRS defaults while the learner's true parameters are unknown until enough revlog exists.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: project on labeled defaults early, log revlog from day one, and refit about monthly so the numbers become the learner's own without stalling the plan

conflict_axes.name: motivating_plan_vs_measured_feasibility
conflict_axes.description: A plan can feel achievable on card counts and motivation while silently breaching the time budget, cutoff, or two-exam split.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: issue a go only when deck-vs-days, load-vs-budget with lapse headroom, the cutoff and the two-exam split all clear; otherwise pull a contingency lever first

edge_cases.description: A default-parameter projection is presented as a personal guarantee of a recall percentage on exam day
edge_cases.trigger: someone reads a default-FSRS load or knowledge estimate as the learner's fitted model before any revlog exists
edge_cases.mitigation: label all pre-fit projections as default-parameter estimates, log revlog from day one, and refit before treating any number as personal

edge_cases.description: An invented days-to-mastery formula is used to promise the deck will be exam-ready by a date
edge_cases.trigger: a single algebraic 'days to learn N cards to retention r' is quoted as if sourced
edge_cases.mitigation: state there is no verified closed-form; obtain time-to-target by FSRS simulation / CMRR or a conservative estimate, clearly labeled

edge_cases.description: The reviews/day cap is set below the steady-state plateau and an invisible overdue backlog grows daily
edge_cases.trigger: a comfortable low review cap is chosen without checking it against the projected plateau
edge_cases.mitigation: set the cap at or above the plateau plus lapse headroom and watch the overdue count as the early-warning signal

edge_cases.description: New cards are introduced right up to the exam so many exam-critical cards are seen only once
edge_cases.mitigation: set the cutoff a derived offset before the exam so every card gets at least one post-graduation review, and cut scope instead of shipping once-seen cards

edge_cases.description: Retention is set to 97%+ 'to be safe' and the daily review load becomes unsustainable
edge_cases.trigger: desired retention is pushed into the steep zone above 90% without checking the workload
edge_cases.mitigation: hold retention near the 0.90 default / CMRR and only nudge up in the final stretch if the budget has slack

edge_cases.description: The plan budgets only first-pass reviews and lapse/relearning churn overflows the daily time
edge_cases.trigger: no relearning headroom is reserved above the plateau
edge_cases.mitigation: reserve review headroom for a lapse fraction from the learner's grade history and reformulate or suspend leeches

edge_cases.description: A multi-day absence returns a large overdue pile that is cleared in one punishing session
edge_cases.trigger: a backlog is drained all at once instead of over several days
edge_cases.mitigation: drain overdue over several days under a raised-but-bounded cap, most-overdue first, relying on days-late credit so recalls are not wasted

edge_cases.description: A dental crunch week starves the TOEFL deck and its reviews silently go overdue
edge_cases.trigger: the shared time budget is blocked on one exam instead of interleaved
edge_cases.mitigation: interleave both decks daily with a demand-weighted split and keep at least a maintenance review slice for the non-priority exam

edge_cases.description: The learner reviews ahead habitually to feel productive and burns capacity for little stability gain
edge_cases.trigger: early review is used as routine progress rather than for logistics
edge_cases.mitigation: default to on-time review and reserve reviewing ahead for a known unavailable stretch or genuinely shaky cards

edge_cases.description: A homegrown or spreadsheet scheduler introduces cohorts deterministically and manufactures recurring same-day spikes
edge_cases.trigger: no interval jitter is added so same-day graded cohorts resurface together
edge_cases.mitigation: add fuzz comparable to Anki's banded jitter and avoid deterministic large same-day batching

edge_cases.description: A custom revlog schema diverges from Anki's and breaks FSRS optimization or insertReviews import
edge_cases.trigger: review data is logged in a shape that does not match the (timestamp, id, grade, interval, last_interval, duration, type) row
edge_cases.mitigation: log exactly in revlog shape with 1-4 grades and validate a round-trip import before relying on it

workflow.action: Fix the memory model and the exam anchor
workflow.description: State scheduling as a (grade, elapsed) -> interval function, define R/S and the forgetting curve, and fix the exam date and days-available as the back-planning origin
workflow.gate: the grade-and-time function, S = interval-at-R=90%, and the exam date with days-available are stated, with no invented days-to-mastery formula

workflow.action: Set desired retention as the workload knob
workflow.description: Give the interval = inverse-curve-at-r identity, the U-shaped workload and the CMRR floor, and the 0.90 default with the >97% warning
workflow.gate: the identity, the U-shaped relationship, the CMRR floor and the log-ratio +5-point cost are stated

workflow.action: Inventory the deck against the days
workflow.description: Count total/new/known cards per exam deck and derive the minimum new-cards/day and the mature-card review baseline
workflow.gate: actual counts per deck yield the deck-vs-days minimum-rate ratio with any estimated portion flagged

workflow.description: Set minutes/day times measured throughput as the shared capacity ceiling across both exams
workflow.gate: the max clearable cards/day is stated as a measured, shared ceiling, not assumed

workflow.description: Express mature reviews/day as deck-size over average interval plus a recurring stream per new card, labeled an estimate pending fitted parameters
workflow.gate: the plateau projection is expressed and labeled an estimate on default parameters

workflow.action: Set the new-card rate and the daily caps
workflow.description: Bound the new-card rate above by matured load/time and below by deck-vs-days, then set the new/day and max-reviews/day caps with a front-load-then-taper shape
workflow.gate: the rate is bounded both ways, the review cap sits at or above the plateau plus lapse headroom, and infeasibility is flagged when the minimum exceeds the sustainable rate

workflow.action: Choose the deadline retention and the last-day-to-learn cutoff
workflow.description: Pick retention between the CMRR floor and the budget ceiling with a moderate-then-nudge ramp, and set the cutoff so every card gets a post-graduation review
workflow.gate: retention sits in range with the ramp tagged estimate, and the cutoff leaves each card at least one post-graduation review

workflow.action: Reserve backlog, lapse and fuzz handling
workflow.description: Reserve relearning headroom, plan gradual backlog draining with days-late credit, and rely on built-in fuzz to disperse cohorts
workflow.gate: relearning headroom is reserved, backlog drains gradually most-overdue-first, and fuzz reliance / custom-jitter requirement is stated

workflow.action: Interleave the two exams and set the early-review and cram posture
workflow.description: Keep separate presets, split the shared minutes by demand, default to on-time review, and bound final-week cram to weak/high-yield cards
workflow.gate: separate presets with a demand-weighted daily split fit the single budget, early review is logistics-only, and cram is bounded and non-substitutive

workflow.action: Instrument the plan and fit parameters
workflow.description: Log every review in revlog shape and fit the FSRS parameters per user from that log, using labeled defaults until enough history exists
workflow.gate: reviews are logged in exact revlog shape feeding the optimizer, with parameters marked UNKNOWN-until-fit and defaults labeled

workflow.description: Burn down remaining new cards and sum-of-R knowledge against days-remaining and pull the ordered contingency levers on divergence
workflow.gate: both curves are tracked against the fixed date using observed retention, and divergence triggers the ordered lever set excluding sub-CMRR retention

workflow.description: Intersect deck-vs-days, load-vs-budget with lapse headroom, the cutoff, the two-exam split and retention-in-range into a go/no-go with the do-not rules
workflow.gate: every constraint clears for a go, the do-not rules are stated, and any breach is a no-go until a contingency lever is pulled

dominance_rules.rule: The daily time budget dominates the desired retention target
dominance_rules.rationale: time/day is a hard capacity while retention is a knob, and workload rises fast above 90%
dominance_rules.trigger: a retention choice projects a load above the daily minutes
dominance_rules.action: cap retention between the CMRR floor and the budget ceiling rather than overflowing the time budget

dominance_rules.rule: Sustainable matured load dominates fast new-card introduction
dominance_rules.rationale: each new card is a recurring review liability, not a one-day cost
dominance_rules.trigger: the new-card rate is set to clear the backlog faster than its matured reviews can be sustained
dominance_rules.action: cap the new-card rate at the level whose matured stream fits the daily budget and taper toward the cutoff

dominance_rules.rule: The spaced review stream dominates final-week cram
dominance_rules.rationale: massed practice underperforms spaced (70% vs 53% immediately post-training; effect size 0.46), and the durable-retention case rests on the spacing-effect direction plus the ESTIMATE-tagged testing effect
dominance_rules.trigger: cram sessions begin crowding out normal reviews
dominance_rules.action: bound cram to weak/high-yield cards on top of, never instead of, the spaced stream

dominance_rules.rule: The last-day-to-learn cutoff dominates covering every card
dominance_rules.rationale: a card seen only once contributes cramming, not durable memory
dominance_rules.trigger: new cards would be introduced with too few days for a post-graduation review
dominance_rules.action: stop new cards at the cutoff and cut low-yield scope instead of shipping once-seen cards

dominance_rules.rationale: early review while R is high gives little stability gain and wastes capacity
dominance_rules.trigger: early review is used as routine progress
dominance_rules.action: review on time and reserve reviewing ahead for a known absence or shaky cards

dominance_rules.rule: The fitted personal model dominates default parameters once history exists
dominance_rules.rationale: defaults are a generic prior that can misstate an individual's load
dominance_rules.trigger: enough revlog has accumulated to fit the w-vector
dominance_rules.action: refit from the user's revlog (about monthly) and replace labeled default projections

dominance_rules.rule: Reserved relearning headroom dominates a first-pass-only budget
dominance_rules.rationale: lapses add near-term reviews on top of the standing load
dominance_rules.trigger: the daily plan is sized only for first-pass reviews
dominance_rules.action: reserve headroom for a realistic lapse fraction and suspend/reformulate leeches

dominance_rules.rule: The nearer or larger exam dominates the shared budget until its deadline
dominance_rules.rationale: one budget cannot fully serve two decks simultaneously
dominance_rules.trigger: two exams' desired paces exceed the shared minutes
dominance_rules.action: give the priority exam the larger slice until its deadline, keeping a maintenance slice for the other, then reallocate

dominance_rules.rule: Measured feasibility dominates a motivating plan
dominance_rules.rationale: a plan can feel achievable while breaching the budget, cutoff or split
dominance_rules.trigger: a go is proposed on card counts or motivation alone
dominance_rules.action: gate the go on all constraints clearing and pull a contingency lever on any breach

anti_rework_rules.rule: Fix the exam date, days-available and actual card counts before choosing any daily numbers
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a daily plan built on more calendar or fewer cards than really exist, retracted once the true counts surface

anti_rework_rules.rule: Bound the new-card rate by its matured review+time load when it is first set
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a fast new-card start that buries the learner in compounding reviews weeks later and forces a mid-course reset

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the reviews/day cap at or above the steady-state plateau plus lapse headroom from the outset
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a hidden overdue backlog accreting under a too-low cap and surfacing as a crisis near the exam

anti_rework_rules.rule: Reserve relearning headroom for a realistic lapse fraction before committing the daily budget
anti_rework_rules.prevents: lapse churn overflowing a first-pass-only budget and requiring the whole schedule to be re-sized

anti_rework_rules.rule: Set the last-day-to-learn cutoff before scheduling the new-card taper
anti_rework_rules.prevents: introducing exam-critical cards too late to get a post-graduation review, unlearnable after the fact

anti_rework_rules.rule: Log reviews in exact revlog shape and validate a round-trip import from day one
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an un-optimizable, un-portable history that cannot be fitted or imported, forcing data to be re-collected

anti_rework_rules.rule: Keep the two exams as separate presets with a demand-weighted split from the start
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a merged single-preset plan that mis-schedules both decks and has to be untangled later

anti_rework_rules.rule: Label every pre-fit projection as a default-parameter estimate
anti_rework_rules.prevents: default numbers being trusted as personal and a plan being rebuilt when the fitted model contradicts them

iteration_protocol.trigger: enough of the learner's own revlog accumulates to fit FSRS parameters, or a monthly re-optimization is due
iteration_protocol.action: refit the w-vector, replace the labeled default projections, and re-project the steady-state load and burndown

iteration_protocol.trigger: the burndown diverges from the fixed-date pace or a load/lapse spike breaches the plan
iteration_protocol.action: pull the ordered contingency levers (time, retention-to-CMRR, scope, taper/cutoff) and recompute the go/no-go

iteration_protocol.trigger: an exam date moves or the realistic days-available/off-days change
iteration_protocol.action: re-derive the days-available budget, the minimum new-card rate and the cutoff, and re-run the feasibility verdict

iteration_protocol.trigger: the observed lapse fraction or per-card throughput diverges from the reserved assumption
iteration_protocol.action: resize the relearning headroom and the daily caps and re-check the load against the time budget

iteration_protocol.trigger: one exam's deadline passes and frees its share of the daily budget
iteration_protocol.action: re-split the shared minutes toward the remaining exam and raise its new-card or review allocation

iteration_protocol.trigger: a recurring overdue backlog appears despite the caps
iteration_protocol.action: treat it as a signal the review cap or new-card rate is above capacity and drain it gradually while lowering the driver

iteration_protocol.trigger: a new Anki/FSRS version changes the scheduler state, curve form, fuzz ranges or revlog schema
iteration_protocol.action: revalidate the memory model, the smoothing assumptions and the telemetry format against the new source of record

iteration_protocol.trigger: a primary source for the absolute forgetting-curve magnitudes becomes reachable
iteration_protocol.action: replace the UNKNOWN-tagged magnitudes with cited figures and re-examine any recall claims that leaned on the curve shape

priority_rationale: The scheduler state model, forgetting-curve backbone, retention-workload knob and exam-date anchor come first because every load number depends on how memory decays, how retention trades against workload, and how many days the deck must fit inside. The deck inventory, time budget and steady-state load math next turn those foundations into the deck-vs-days ratio, the capacity ceiling and the plateau the plan is sized against. The new-card rate, daily-load shaping, deadline retention target and last-day-to-learn cutoff then set the core pacing decisions. The execution nodes (backlog, lapse budget, fuzz, ahead-review, multi-exam interleaving, cram) make the shaped plan resilient and reconcile the two parallel exams under one budget. The telemetry and parameter-optimization nodes instrument the plan and personalize its model. The burndown, contingency replan and go/no-go come last because they compose every upstream quantity into an on-pace measurement, a bounded correction procedure and a defensible feasibility verdict against the fixed exam date.
